proposed_edges.relationship: Darnton's ‘In Search of the Enlightenment’ (Journal of Modern History, 1971) was a largely critical review of Gay's The Enlightenment, judging his intellectual history old-fashioned and arguing that his dialectical scheme of a classical appeal against Christianity failed: if antiquity was so decisive, why did the Enlightenment not begin in the Renaissance? (as read by Velema 2014 and Edelstein 2012).
proposed_edges.map_label: Social history of ideas against Gay, 1971
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated through two named readers; Darnton's review (JMH 43, 1971, 113–132) is unread. (1) Wyger Velema, ‘Oude waarheden’, Tijdschrift voor Geschiedenis 127:2 (2014), p. 230 and n. 3, read in the published version in the UvA institutional repository (Dutch; paraphrase mine): Darnton's review argued that the form of intellectual history Gay practised was ‘bijzonder ouderwets’ (particularly old-fashioned) and that ‘diens hele dialectische schema niet deugde’; if the classical tradition had mattered so much, why had the Enlightenment not begun in the Renaissance; for Darnton sixteenth- and seventeenth-century thinkers ‘van Bacon tot Newton’ stood at its cradle, and Gay had smuggled them in ‘via een achterdeur’, undermining his thesis; Velema speaks of ‘het scherpe meningsverschil tussen Darnton en Gay’. (2) Dan Edelstein, ‘The Classical Turn in Enlightenment Studies’, Modern Intellectual History 9:1 (2012), 61–71, publisher's opening extract read: ‘Robert Darnton hailed this rising tide of social and cultural history in a 1971 largely critical review of Gay's two volumes’ (n. 2). Page of the Edelstein sentence not visible (opening of the article). Gay's reply, if any, was not searched. Distinct from edge_2720 (Anderson → Darnton).

review.reason: Both readers re-checked. Velema 2014, UvA-DARE published version, p. 230 and n. 3 (Darnton, 'In search of the Enlightenment. Recent attempts to create a social history of ideas', JMH 43, 1971, 113–132): 'bijzonder ouderwets', 'diens hele dialectische schema niet deugde', the Renaissance question, 'van Bacon tot Newton', 'via een achterdeur', 'Het scherpe meningsverschil tussen Darnton en Gay'. Edelstein 2012 (Crossref abstract / Cambridge opening): 'Robert Darnton hailed this rising tide of social and cultural history in a 1971 largely critical review of Gay's two volumes'. Institutional repository and publisher routes. Two independent substantive readers, attributed in the relationship. Accept.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Enlightenment: An Interpretation (1966–69), presented as a ‘social history of ideas’, read the philosophes' appeal to antiquity, tension with Christianity and pursuit of modernity as the beginning of Western modernity, against Carl Becker's secularized-Christianity reading, and became a standard work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A reader's account, read. Velema (2014), pp. 229–230 (UvA repository, published version): Gay's ‘monumentale studie’, ‘door de auteur … gepresenteerd als een proeve van de “social history of ideas”’, in fact a fairly traditional history of ideas treating the Enlightenment as a unity centred on Paris; Gay presented it ‘nadrukkelijk’ as the beginning of Western modernity, opposing Carl Becker's 1932 reading (n. 2); his dialectic of ‘the appeal to antiquity’, ‘the tension with Christianity’ and ‘the pursuit of modernity’; the book ‘groeide uit tot een standaardwerk’ but closed an era rather than opening one. Velema n. 1 cites Gay's methodological essay ‘The social history of ideas: Ernst Cassirer and after’ (in The Critical Spirit, 1967), unread. Publication years agree with the Yale AHA citation already on the atlas (tc234_gay_yale). Gay's volumes are unread. Becker and Cassirer are not atlas endpoints.

review.reason: Velema pp. 229–230 re-read: Gay's 'monumentale studie' presented by the author 'als een proeve van de “social history of ideas”', in fact 'een tamelijk traditionele vorm van ideeëngeschiedenis'; presented 'nadrukkelijk' as the beginning of Western modernity against Becker (n. 2); the appeal to antiquity / tension with Christianity / pursuit of modernity scheme; 'groeide uit tot een standaardwerk'. Relationship matches; evidence note keeps Velema's qualification that the book closed an era. Gay's Enlightenment books are unread, which the note says. Accept.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gay dates his turn to Freud to c. 1950–51 at Columbia, when Franz Neumann, ‘tied to the Frankfurt School’, began a serious reading course on Freud with Herbert Marcuse taking part (Gay 1997).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own retrospective testimony, read. ‘The Psychoanalytically-Informed Historian’ (interview, September 1997; cliospsyche.org excerpt), answer to ‘What brought you to psychohistory?’: ‘an older colleague, Franz Neumann, who was a left-wing Marxist’; ‘Having been tied to the Frankfurt School he had some interest in Freud’; Neumann's circle ‘started this serious course of reading on Freud’, with ‘their best friend, Herbert Marcuse’; Gay calls himself an amateur then and dates professional training to the mid-1970s. The route is social and personal: it does not claim Gay adopted critical theory, and Neumann and Marcuse are not atlas endpoints, so the edge attaches to the group endpoint on Gay's own identification of Neumann with the Frankfurt School. Velema (2014) n. 1 independently records Gay's 1967 methodological essay appearing in a volume of essays in honour of Marcuse. Retrospective recollection, not contemporaneous evidence. Complements edge_2935 (Freud → Gay).

review.reason: cliospsyche.org interview (existing source gay_interview_1997) re-fetched: 'The interest goes back to 1950/1951'; 'an older colleague, Franz Neumann, who was a left-wing Marxist'; 'Having been tied to the Frankfurt School he had some interest in Freud'; Marcuse joined the 'serious course of reading on Freud'; 'This aroused my interest.' Velema n. 1 independently confirms Gay's 1967 essay in The Critical Spirit, essays in honour of Herbert Marcuse. The relationship is bounded to his Freud turn via a Frankfurt-associated circle and explicitly does not claim adoption of critical theory. Retrospective testimony, so stated. Accept.
